dateNotes: There is no single 'arrival date': its encounters were flybys of Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).
The mission was continuing ('Extended Mission') at the last review, so the last-contact and mission-end dates are empty.
NASA's page gives two dates for entering interstellar space (November 25 and December 10, 2018), so we write 'November–December 2018'.

status.text: Still operating in an 'Extended Mission' in interstellar space (as of the last review) — check NASA's page for current status

location.description: In interstellar space, outside the heliosphere. It is not at Uranus or Neptune.

primary.title: A free push from gravity
primary.howItWorks: When Voyager 2 passes close to a planet, the planet's gravity pulls on it and changes its path and speed, flinging it toward the next planet.
primary.knowledge: With this trick it visited four giant planets in one trip, and we saw Uranus and Neptune up close for the first time.

secondary.title: The magnetometer at Uranus: the surprise of the tilt
secondary.howItWorks: The magnetometer recorded the direction and strength of the magnetic field along the short flyby path, and scientists reconstructed the shape of the field around the planet from it.
secondary.knowledge: Result: a field tilted about 55 degrees from the rotation axis and offset from the planet's center — challenging models that assume a centered field nearly aligned with the axis.

engineeringChallenge.challenge: The farther the spacecraft went, the weaker its signal at Earth, and the close-study window was very short (about 5.5 hours at Uranus).
engineeringChallenge.solution: The Deep Space Network's largest antennas were enlarged from 64 to 70 meters before the Neptune encounter, and each flyby was planned precisely to use the few close hours.

discoveries.text: At Uranus: 10 new moons and two new rings.
Uranus's magnetic field is tilted about 55 degrees and offset from the center.
At Neptune: new moons and rings, and the 'Great Dark Spot'.
Its images remain a baseline for measuring how the atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune change over time.

timeline.text: Uranus flyby — the only spacecraft to visit it.
Neptune flyby — the only spacecraft to visit it.
Crosses the termination shock at the edge of the heliosphere.
Enters interstellar space (NASA gives two different dates).
Begins using trajectory-correction thrusters for pointing instead of its aging attitude thrusters.

chapters.text: I am Voyager 2. I launched in 1977, and I am still traveling today! I am the only spacecraft that has visited Uranus and Neptune.
I was sent to visit the faraway giant planets. In those years, their positions let me hop from one planet to the next.
I never landed on any planet. I zoomed past each one, taking pictures and measurements, and then its gravity helped fling me toward the next planet.
At Uranus I discovered new moons and rings. At Neptune I saw a big dark storm that scientists named the 'Great Dark Spot'.
After Neptune I kept going, and now I am in the space between the stars, outside the Sun's bubble. I left nothing behind on Uranus or Neptune.

glossary.meaning: Passing close to a planet without landing on it or circling it.
The force that pulls things toward a planet.

chapters.text: I am Voyager 2, launched on August 20, 1977. I flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1981, then was sent on to Uranus and Neptune. I am still the only spacecraft to have visited those two planets, and every encounter I made was a flyby — never a landing, never an orbit.

Extending my route to Uranus and Neptune was conditional: if Voyager 1 succeeded at its goals, I could be redirected using gravity-assist maneuvers. The trip from Saturn to Uranus took about four and a half years.

At Uranus I had only about 5.5 hours for close study, with closest approach on January 24, 1986, at about 81,500 kilometers. Because signals weaken with distance, the Deep Space Network's largest antennas were enlarged from 64 to 70 meters before the Neptune encounter.

At Uranus I discovered 10 new moons and two rings, and a magnetic field tilted about 55 degrees from the rotation axis and offset from the center. At Neptune, on August 25, 1989, I discovered moons, rings and the 'Great Dark Spot'. My images are still a baseline for comparing how both planets' weather changes.

I am not at Uranus or Neptune today. I crossed the termination shock in 2007 and entered interstellar space in late 2018. NASA lists me as an 'Extended Mission', but my power keeps declining, and engineers are making difficult choices about instruments and thrusters. My status changes, so check NASA's page.

glossary.meaning: A boundary where the solar wind suddenly slows down, before the edge of the heliosphere.
The region outside the bubble of particles and magnetic fields blown out by the Sun.

task.q: About how much time passed between the Uranus flyby and the Neptune flyby?
task.explanation: From January 1986 to August 1989 is about three years and seven months. Distances between the outer planets are enormous.

questions.q: Why were the Deep Space Network antennas enlarged before the Neptune encounter?
options: To catch a weaker signal coming from farther away
To send fuel to the spacecraft
questions.explanation: A larger dish collects more signal energy, so more data can be received with fewer errors.

questions.q: NASA's page says 'five new moons' at Neptune in one place and 'six' in another. What is the correct scientific response?
options: Check other primary sources and document the discrepancy instead of picking a number at random
Pick the bigger number because it is more exciting
questions.explanation: Even reliable sources can contain inconsistencies. That is why this site says 'new moons' without a number until it is resolved.

questions.q: 'Uranus's field is tilted about 55 degrees.' This statement is…
options: A result measured by the magnetometer
Information from a spacecraft that landed on Uranus
questions.explanation: The measurement came from the flyby itself; no spacecraft has landed on Uranus.

verificationNotes: Operating status changes over time; this reflects NASA's page at review time. We do not state the number of working instruments or the current distance because they change and were not verified from a primary source.
